final_proof:
**Conventions.** Throughout, $I=[a,b]$ with $a\le b$, so $I\neq\varnothing$. A function $f:I\to\mathbb R$ is *continuous on $I$* if for every $x_0\in I$ and every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $\delta>0$ such that $|f(x)-f(x_0)|<\varepsilon$ for all $x\in I$ with $|x-x_0|<\delta$. (At $x_0=a$ or $x_0=b$ this is exactly one-sided continuity, the usual convention for $C[a,b]$.) $C(I)$ is the set of all such functions. For $f,g:I\to\mathbb R$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb R$, the pointwise operations are $(f+g)(x)=f(x)+g(x)$ and $(\lambda\cdot f)(x)=\lambda f(x)$ for $x\in I$. Two functions $I\to\mathbb R$ are equal iff they take the same value at every $x\in I$.

We must show: (A) $+$ and $\cdot$ are well-defined operations $C(I)\times C(I)\to C(I)$ and $\mathbb R\times C(I)\to C(I)$ (closure); (B) $(C(I),+)$ is an abelian group; (C) the four scalar-multiplication axioms hold.

---

**(A) Closure.**

*Lemma 1.* If $f,g\in C(I)$ then $f+g\in C(I)$.

*Proof.* Let $x_0\in I$, $\varepsilon>0$. Choose $\delta_1>0$ with $|f(x)-f(x_0)|<\varepsilon/2$ for $x\in I$, $|x-x_0|<\delta_1$, and $\delta_2>0$ with $|g(x)-g(x_0)|<\varepsilon/2$ for $x\in I$, $|x-x_0|<\delta_2$. Put $\delta=\min(\delta_1,\delta_2)>0$. For $x\in I$ with $|x-x_0|<\delta$, by the triangle inequality
$$|(f+g)(x)-(f+g)(x_0)| \le |f(x)-f(x_0)|+|g(x)-g(x_0)|<\tfrac\varepsilon2+\tfrac\varepsilon2=\varepsilon. \qquad\blacksquare$$

*Lemma 2.* If $f\in C(I)$ and $\lambda\in\mathbb R$ then $\lambda\cdot f\in C(I)$.

*Proof.* Let $x_0\in I$, $\varepsilon>0$. Since $|\lambda|+1>0$, choose $\delta>0$ with $|f(x)-f(x_0)|<\varepsilon/(|\lambda|+1)$ for $x\in I$, $|x-x_0|<\delta$. Then for such $x$,
$$|\lambda f(x)-\lambda f(x_0)| = |\lambda|\,|f(x)-f(x_0)| \le (|\lambda|+1)\,|f(x)-f(x_0)| < \varepsilon.\qquad\blacksquare$$

Hence $+:C(I)\times C(I)\to C(I)$ and $\cdot:\mathbb R\times C(I)\to C(I)$ are well-defined.

**(B) $(C(I),+)$ is an abelian group.** Let $f,g,h\in C(I)$.

1. *Associativity.* For each $x\in I$: $((f+g)+h)(x)=(f(x)+g(x))+h(x)=f(x)+(g(x)+h(x))=(f+(g+h))(x)$, by associativity of $+_\mathbb R$. So $(f+g)+h=f+(g+h)$.
2. *Commutativity.* For each $x\in I$: $(f+g)(x)=f(x)+g(x)=g(x)+f(x)=(g+f)(x)$. So $f+g=g+f$.
3. *Identity.* Let $0_I:I\to\mathbb R$, $0_I(x)=0$. It is continuous on $I$: for any $x_0,\varepsilon$, any $\delta>0$ works since $|0_I(x)-0_I(x_0)|=0<\varepsilon$. So $0_I\in C(I)$, and $(f+0_I)(x)=f(x)+0=f(x)$ for all $x$, so $f+0_I=f$ (and $0_I+f=f$ by 2).
4. *Inverses.* Define $-f:=(-1)\cdot f$, i.e. $(-f)(x)=-f(x)$. By Lemma 2, $-f\in C(I)$. For all $x\in I$: $(f+(-f))(x)=f(x)+(-f(x))=0=0_I(x)$, so $f+(-f)=0_I$ (and $(-f)+f=0_I$ by 2).

**(C) Scalar axioms.** Let $f,g\in C(I)$, $\lambda,\mu\in\mathbb R$. Each identity is checked at an arbitrary $x\in I$ using the field axioms of $\mathbb R$; since both sides lie in $C(I)$ by (A) and agree at every point, they are equal as elements of $C(I)$.

5. $\lambda\cdot(f+g)=\lambda\cdot f+\lambda\cdot g$: $\lambda(f(x)+g(x))=\lambda f(x)+\lambda g(x)$ (distributivity in $\mathbb R$).
6. $(\lambda+\mu)\cdot f=\lambda\cdot f+\mu\cdot f$: $(\lambda+\mu)f(x)=\lambda f(x)+\mu f(x)$ (distributivity in $\mathbb R$).
7. $(\lambda\mu)\cdot f=\lambda\cdot(\mu\cdot f)$: $(\lambda\mu)f(x)=\lambda(\mu f(x))$ (associativity of $\times_\mathbb R$).
8. $1\cdot f=f$: $1\cdot f(x)=f(x)$ ($1$ is the multiplicative identity of $\mathbb R$).

**Conclusion.** $C(I)$ is closed under pointwise addition and under pointwise multiplication by real scalars (A); $(C(I),+)$ is an abelian group with zero $0_I$ and inverses $-f$ (B); and the scalar multiplication satisfies both distributive laws, compatibility with field multiplication, and the unit law (C). These are precisely the vector space axioms over the field $(\mathbb R,+_\mathbb R,\times_\mathbb R)$. Hence $(C(I),+,\cdot)_\mathbb R$ is a vector space. $\blacksquare$

*Remark.* The argument never used that $I$ is an interval or closed; it only used that the operations are pointwise and that continuity (relative to $I$) is preserved by sums and scalar multiples. (If one allowed $a>b$ so $I=\varnothing$, $C(I)$ would consist of the single empty function, which is the zero vector space, so the claim still holds.)
